newsitem.title: UK: Cameroon raises 95/96 cocoa estimate to 132,000 T.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon raises 95/96 cocoa estimate to 132,000 T.

text.p: Cameroon has raised its 1995/96 cocoa crop estimate to 132,000 tonnes from its earlier forecast of 120,000 tonnes, a senior government official said.

"We cannot explain the increase but the increase was there," Hope Sona Ebai, director-general of Cameroon's National Cocoa and Coffee Board, told Reuters at the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) meeting.
But he hoped production would be capped at 120,000 tonnes a year until 1999 when the current five-year cocoa agreement, administered by the London-based ICCO, expires.
"I think the production should be stable at least through the life of the agreement," he said.
The ICCO put production from the African state at 120,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
Sona Ebai said high start-up costs for cocoa cultivation in Cameroon have deterred new investments in the sector.
He said the growing emphasis on crop diversification, market liberalisation and the abolition of farm subsidies might also encourage farmers to move away from cocoa.
"I don't see a fantastic increase in production," he said.

"The beginning costs of plantations are also prohibitive. Governments used to assist with some kind of premiums for people going into medium-sized farms of 20 hectares each but those things are gone now because of financial reasons and policy reasons," he said.
Cocoa exports from Cameroon, a small producer compared with its neighbours Ivory Coast and Ghana, normally come up to between 90,000 and 100,000 tonnes a year, Sona Ebai said.
Average cocoa yield is around 600 kg per hectare a year. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
